VERIFIED SOURCES:
[SRC:CPA2019-S2-47-viii]
Source: Section 2(47)(viii), The Consumer Protection Act, 2019 (35 of 2019)
Status: In force.
Official wording: refusing, after selling goods or rendering services, to take back or withdraw defective goods or to withdraw or discontinue deficient services and to refund the consideration thereof, if paid, within the period stipulated in the bill or cash memo or receipt or in the absence of such stipulation, within a period of thirty days
Plain explanation: Refusing to take back defective goods, or to stop deficient services, and refund the money is listed as an unfair trade practice. The time limit is the period stated in the bill or receipt. If none is stated, it is thirty days.

[SRC:ECOM2020-R6-3]
Source: Rule 6(3), Consumer Protection (E-Commerce) Rules, 2020, G.S.R. 462(E)
Status: In force.
Official wording: No seller offering goods or services through a marketplace e -commerce entity shall refuse to take back goods, or withdraw or discontinue services purchased or agreed to be purchased, or refuse to refund consideration, if paid, if such goods or services are defective, deficient or spurious, or if the goods or services are not of the characteristics or features as advertised or as agreed to, or if such goods or services are delivered late from the stated delivery schedule | Provided that in the case of late delivery, this sub -rule shall not be applied if such late delivery was due to force majeure
Plain explanation: A marketplace seller must not refuse to take back goods or refund the money if the goods or services are defective, deficient, spurious, different from what was advertised or agreed, or delivered late. Late delivery caused by force majeure is an exception.

[SRC:CPA2019-S2-10]
Source: Section 2(10), The Consumer Protection Act, 2019 (35 of 2019)
Status: In force.
Official wording: “defect” means any fault, imperfection or shortcoming in the quality, quantity, potency, purity or standard which is required to be maintained by or under any law for the time being in force or under any contract, express or implied or as is claimed by the trader in any manner whatsoever in relation to any goods or product
Plain explanation: A defect is a fault or shortcoming in the quality or quantity of goods, measured against what the law requires, what a contract promises, or what the trader claimed.

[SRC:ECOM2020-R4-10]
Source: Rule 4(10), Consumer Protection (E-Commerce) Rules, 2020, G.S.R. 462(E)
Status: In force.
Official wording: Every e-commerce entity shall effect all payments towards accepted refund requests of the consumers as prescribed by the Reserve Bank of India or any other competent authority under any law for the time being in force, within a reasonable period of time, or as prescribed under applicable laws
Plain explanation: Once a refund request is accepted, an online platform must pay it within a reasonable time, or within the time set by the Reserve Bank of India or other applicable law. This rule does not itself state a fixed number of days.

[SRC:ECOM2020-R2-1]
Source: Rule 2(1), Consumer Protection (E-Commerce) Rules, 2020, G.S.R. 462(E)
Status: In force.
Official wording: all goods and services bought or sold over digital or electronic network including digital products | all models of e-commerce, including marketplace and inventory models of e-commerce
Plain explanation: The E-Commerce Rules apply to goods and services bought or sold online, including digital products, and to both marketplace and inventory models.

[SRC:ECOM2020-R4-8]
Source: Rule 4(8), Consumer Protection (E-Commerce) Rules, 2020, G.S.R. 462(E)
Status: In force.
Official wording: No e -commerce entity shall impose cancellation charges on consumers cancelling after confirming purchase unless similar charges are also borne by the e - commerce entity, if they cancel the purchase order unilaterally for any reason
Plain explanation: An online platform cannot charge a consumer for cancelling after confirming a purchase, unless the platform also bears similar charges when it cancels an order on its own.

VERIFIED SOURCES:
[SRC:EJAGRITI-LIMITATION-DOCS]
Source: e-Jagriti: Consumer Complaint (CC) Workflow: Consumer Complaint workflow
Status: In force.
Official wording: Mandatory Documents -Index -Proforma for Filing CC -Synopsis with List of Dates and Events -Memo of Parties -CC with Notarised affidavit -Add Annexures / Documents -Add Application (IA) -Vakalatnama | Filed within the period of 2 Yrs of cause of action
Plain explanation: The official e-Jagriti workflow lists the documents for filing a consumer complaint, including a synopsis with dates and events, a memo of parties and a notarised affidavit. Check the portal's current list, because it may change.

[SRC:CPA2019-S2-11]
Source: Section 2(11), The Consumer Protection Act, 2019 (35 of 2019)
Status: In force.
Official wording: “deficiency” means any fault, imperfection, shortcoming or inadequacy in the quality, nature and manner of performance which is required to be maintained by or under any law for the time being in force or has been undertaken to be performed by a person in pursuance of a contract or otherwise in relation to any service
Plain explanation: A deficiency is a fault or inadequacy in how a service is performed, measured against what the law requires or what the provider undertook to do. Failing to deliver a promised service may fall within this meaning, depending on the facts.

[SRC:ECOM2020-R5-3-a]
Source: Rule 5(3)(a), Consumer Protection (E-Commerce) Rules, 2020, G.S.R. 462(E)
Status: In force.
Official wording: a marketplace e -commerce entity shall, on a request in writing made by a consumer after the purchase of any goods or services on its platform by such consumer, provide him with information regarding the seller from which such consumer has made such purchase
Plain explanation: After a purchase, a consumer can ask a marketplace in writing for the seller's details, so that the consumer can contact the seller to resolve the dispute.

[SRC:CPA2019-S38-7]
Source: Section 38(7), The Consumer Protection Act, 2019 (35 of 2019)
Status: In force.
Official wording: Every complaint shall be disposed of as expeditiously as possible and endeavour shall be made to decide the complaint within a period of three months from the date of receipt of notice by opposite party where the complaint does not require analysis or testing of commodities and within five months if it requires analysis or testing of commodities
Plain explanation: The Commission should try to decide a complaint within three months of the opposite party receiving notice, or five months if goods need testing. This is a target, not a guarantee.

[SRC:CPA2019-S37-1]
Source: Section 37(1), The Consumer Protection Act, 2019 (35 of 2019)
Status: In force.
Official wording: if it appears to the District Commission that there exists elements of a settlement which may be acceptable to the parties, except in such cases as may be prescribed, it may direct the parties to give in writing, within five days, consent to have their dispute settled by mediation
Plain explanation: If a settlement looks possible, the District Commission may ask both sides whether they agree in writing to try mediation. Some cases are excluded.

[SRC:CPA2019-S2-28]
Source: Section 2(28), The Consumer Protection Act, 2019 (35 of 2019)
Status: In force.

Higher bands are in the rule. Check the fee shown on e-Jagriti before filing.

[SRC:CPA2019-S34-2]
Source: Section 34(2), The Consumer Protection Act, 2019 (35 of 2019)
Status: In force.
Official wording: the complainant resides or personally works for gain | the cause of action, wholly or in part, arises | A complaint shall be instituted in a District Commission within the local limits of whose jurisdiction
Plain explanation: A complaint can be filed in the District Commission for the area where the opposite party lives or does business, where the cause of action arose in whole or part, or where the complainant lives or works.

[SRC:ECOM2020-R5-3-b]
Source: Rule 5(3)(b), Consumer Protection (E-Commerce) Rules, 2020, G.S.R. 462(E)
Status: In force.
Official wording: a ticket number for each complaint lodged through which the consumer can track the status of the complaint
Plain explanation: A marketplace must provide a ticket number for each complaint, so the consumer can track its status. Keep this number as evidence.

[SRC:CPA2019-S69]
Source: Section 69, The Consumer Protection Act, 2019 (35 of 2019)
Status: In force.
Official wording: The District Commission, the State Commission or the National Commission shall not admit a complaint unless it is filed within two years from the date on which the cause of action has arisen | a complaint may be entertained after the period specified in sub -section ( 1), if the complainant satisfies the District Commission, the State Commission or the National Commission, as the case may be, that he had sufficient cause for not filing the complaint within such period
Plain explanation: A complaint must generally be filed within two years from the date the cause of action arose. A late complaint may be accepted only if the Commission is satisfied there was sufficient cause for the delay. Working out the start date can be difficult, so check it with a lawyer if time may be short.

[SRC:NCH-CONTACT]
Source: National Consumer Helpline: official website: Helpline contact details
Status: In force.
Official wording: Toll Free 1915 (8AM to 8PM) | WhatsApp +918800001915 | Call National Consumer Helpline at 1915 or 1800114000 | Register your consumer grievance through the NCH Web Portal, Mobile App, UMANG, WhatsApp or Call Centre.
Plain explanation: The National Consumer Helpline can be reached on toll-free 1915 (8 AM to 8 PM) or 1800114000, or on WhatsApp at +918800001915. A grievance can be registered through its web portal, mobile app, UMANG, WhatsApp or call centre.
